definitions.definition: The study of God's character using the laws of physics.
definitions.example: Like using a microscope to see how a watch works, then guessing who made it.

definitions.definition: A formal project to study a specific topic.
definitions.example: A school science fair project, but bigger and with more rules.

definitions.definition: The official or standard version of something.
definitions.example: The original recipe for a dish, not a copycat version.

definitions.definition: A detailed description or picture of someone's character.
definitions.example: A police sketch of a suspect, but for personality traits.

definitions.definition: The four basic ways particles in the universe interact: gravity, electromagnetism, strong nuclear, and weak nuclear.
definitions.example: Like the four basic rules of a video game that control everything that happens.

definitions.definition: Builds up or gathers over time.
definitions.example: Saving pennies in a jar until you have a lot.

definitions.definition: A force that pulls objects with mass toward each other.
definitions.example: What makes an apple fall from a tree and keeps the Moon orbiting Earth.

definitions.definition: Unearned kindness or help from God.
definitions.example: Getting a second chance on a test you didn't study for.

definitions.definition: Formed or influenced something's structure.
definitions.example: How wind shapes sand dunes over time.

definitions.definition: Protected or blocked from something, like radiation or a force.
definitions.example: A lead apron at the dentist's office blocks X-rays.

definitions.definition: Pulling things together, not pushing them apart.
definitions.example: A magnet pulling a paperclip is attractive.

definitions.definition: Pushing things apart.
definitions.example: Two magnets with the same poles facing each other push apart.

definitions.definition: A force that works across any distance, no matter how far.
definitions.example: Gravity from a star billions of light-years away still pulls on you, just very weakly.

definitions.definition: Changing the direction something moves by bending the space around it.
definitions.example: A bowling ball on a trampoline makes a marble roll in a curve around it.

definitions.definition: Sudden, sharp increases.
definitions.example: A spike in temperature during a heatwave.

definitions.definition: The strongest force in nature, which holds the center of atoms together.
definitions.example: The glue that keeps the tiny particles in an atom's core from flying apart.

definitions.definition: A deep, caring attachment that seeks the best for someone else.
definitions.example: A parent caring for a child no matter what.

definitions.definition: The property of the strong force that gets stronger as particles are pulled apart, trapping them together.
definitions.example: Like trying to pull apart two magnets stuck together—the harder you pull, the harder they stick.

definitions.definition: The strong force is weak when particles are very close, giving them freedom to move.
definitions.example: A loose leash lets a dog wander nearby, but a tight leash yanks it back.

definitions.definition: The tiny, dense center of an atom, made of protons and neutrons.
definitions.example: The pit of a peach, but for an atom.

definitions.definition: The scale of individual atoms, the smallest units of matter.
definitions.example: Zooming in so far you can see single atoms.

definitions.definition: A grid of numbers that shows how different things are connected and affect each other.
definitions.example: A spreadsheet that tracks how changing one thing, like price, affects everything else, like sales and profit.

definitions.definition: How strongly two forces or particles interact with each other.
definitions.example: How tightly two magnets are stuck together.

definitions.definition: Math equations that describe how things change over time or space.
definitions.example: An equation that predicts how fast a cup of coffee cools down.

definitions.definition: A measure of disorder or randomness in a system.
definitions.example: Your bedroom naturally gets messier over time unless you clean it.

definitions.definition: When waves are perfectly aligned, working together to create a stronger effect.
definitions.example: A laser beam is coherent light—all the light waves march in step.

definitions.definition: A force that involves electricity and magnetism, and is responsible for light and most everyday interactions.
definitions.example: What makes magnets stick to your fridge and your phone work.

definitions.definition: What is real and correct, not false or deceptive.
definitions.example: Saying the sky is blue when it is actually blue.

definitions.definition: Travels or spreads through space.
definitions.example: Sound propagates through air from a speaker to your ear.

definitions.definition: A substance or material that something travels through.
definitions.example: Air is the medium for sound; water is the medium for waves in a pool.

definitions.definition: Able to keep itself going without outside help.
definitions.example: A plant that makes its own food through sunlight.

definitions.definition: Breaks down or gets worse over time.
definitions.example: An old photograph degrades and becomes faded.

definitions.definition: A tiny particle of light.
definitions.example: A single speck of light from a flashlight.

definitions.definition: The light-sensitive layer at the back of your eye.
definitions.example: The screen at the back of a camera that captures the image.

definitions.definition: Four math rules that describe how electricity and magnetism work together to create light.
definitions.example: The instruction manual for how light and radio waves behave.

definitions.definition: Brought together into one thing.
definitions.example: Merging two school clubs into one bigger club.

definitions.definition: Different viewpoints or perspectives, especially in physics (like moving vs. standing still).
definitions.example: Watching a car race from the stands vs. from inside a car.

definitions.definition: The idea that mass and energy are two forms of the same thing, related by E=mc².
definitions.example: A tiny amount of matter can be turned into a huge amount of energy, like in a nuclear bomb.

definitions.definition: Importance or meaning.
definitions.example: The significance of a birthday is that you're another year older.

definitions.definition: Einstein's famous equation: Energy equals mass times the speed of light squared.
definitions.example: It means a little bit of stuff can become a huge amount of energy.

definitions.definition: A number you multiply by to change one unit into another.
definitions.example: Multiplying inches by 2.54 converts them to centimeters.

definitions.definition: Extremely surprising or shocking.
definitions.example: The cost of a new phone can be staggering.

definitions.definition: Not moving or not able to react.
definitions.example: A rock sitting on the ground is inert.

definitions.definition: A large amount of something that is not obvious.
definitions.example: A small seed contains the hidden magnitude of a giant tree.

definitions.definition: The study of heat, energy, and how things change, especially the tendency toward disorder.
definitions.example: Why ice melts in a warm room and why you can't un-burn a piece of toast.

definitions.definition: Something that must happen and cannot be avoided.
definitions.example: It is a necessity that you need water to live.

definitions.definition: A system that does not exchange energy or matter with its surroundings.
definitions.example: A sealed, insulated thermos is a closed system.

definitions.definition: A state of being messy or random, measured by entropy.
definitions.example: A shuffled deck of cards has more disorder than a sorted one.

definitions.definition: The one-way direction of time from past to future, linked to increasing disorder.
definitions.example: You can remember yesterday but not tomorrow.

definitions.definition: When a system naturally becomes more ordered without outside help.
definitions.example: Snowflakes forming complex shapes as they fall.

definitions.definition: Happening naturally, without being forced.
definitions.example: A balloon popping spontaneously when it gets too full.

definitions.definition: Energy that comes from outside a system.
definitions.example: Plugging a phone into a wall outlet provides external energy input.

definitions.definition: The rule that erasing information always costs energy and creates heat.
definitions.example: Deleting a file on a computer uses a tiny bit of energy.

definitions.definition: Proof or record of something happening.
definitions.example: A store receipt proves you bought something.

definitions.definition: Making a small part of a system more ordered, even though the whole becomes more disordered.
definitions.example: Cleaning your room (making it more ordered) while the rest of the house gets messier.

definitions.definition: A process or method that makes something happen.
definitions.example: A lock's mechanism uses a key to open it.

definitions.definition: The law of thermodynamics that says disorder always increases in a closed system.
definitions.example: Your room will get messier on its own, never cleaner.

definitions.definition: The study of how information is measured, stored, and sent, especially through noisy channels.
definitions.example: How your phone compresses a photo to send it faster.

definitions.definition: A title for Jesus in the Bible, meaning the ultimate message or logic from God.
definitions.example: Like the 'word' in 'give me your word'—a promise that creates reality.

definitions.definition: Claude Shannon, a scientist who created information theory and defined the maximum rate of data transmission.
definitions.example: The person who figured out the fastest speed you can send a text without errors.

definitions.definition: The fastest possible speed at which something can happen.
definitions.example: The maximum rate you can fill a bathtub is limited by how fast water comes out of the faucet.

definitions.definition: Sent or passed from one place to another.
definitions.example: A radio signal is transmitted from a tower to your car.

definitions.definition: A path for sending information that has interference or errors.
definitions.example: A bad phone line with static is a noisy channel.

definitions.definition: Andrey Kolmogorov, a mathematician who defined the shortest possible description of something.
definitions.example: The shortest instruction manual that can perfectly describe a Lego model.

definitions.definition: The shortest set of instructions needed to create a specific output.
definitions.example: The fewest words to describe a picture so someone can draw it exactly.

definitions.definition: A very ordered, non-random condition with high information content.
definitions.example: A perfectly stacked pile of books has low entropy.

definitions.definition: Converting information into a specific form for storage or transmission.
definitions.example: Turning a song into MP3 format is encoding.

definitions.definition: The maximum amount of information that can be sent through a communication path.
definitions.example: The number of cars a bridge can hold at once.

definitions.definition: Copied exactly.
definitions.example: Making a photocopy of a document clones it.

definitions.definition: Damaged or made incorrect.
definitions.example: A corrupted computer file won't open properly.

definitions.definition: The most basic, underlying layer of reality.
definitions.example: Atoms are at the fundamental level of matter.

definitions.definition: To develop or become revealed over time.
definitions.example: A story unfolds as you read more chapters.

definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that the laws of physics are the same for all observers, and that time and space can change depending on motion.
definitions.example: A clock on a fast spaceship ticks slower than one on Earth.

definitions.definition: Being reliable and keeping promises no matter what.
definitions.example: A dog that waits for its owner every day is faithful.

definitions.definition: A viewpoint from which you measure things like speed and position.
definitions.example: Watching a ball from a moving train vs. standing on the ground are different reference frames.

definitions.definition: Events that happen at the same time from one viewpoint, but may not from another.
definitions.example: Two fireworks exploding at the same time might look different to someone far away.

definitions.definition: A measurement that combines space and time and stays the same for all observers.
definitions.example: The 'distance' between two events that doesn't change, even if people disagree on time or location.

definitions.definition: Something that does not change, even when other things do.
definitions.example: The total number of pieces in a puzzle is invariant, even if you rearrange them.

definitions.definition: The idea that being in a gravitational field feels the same as accelerating.
definitions.example: In a windowless elevator, you can't tell if you're going up or if gravity is pulling you down.

definitions.definition: The study of shapes, sizes, and the properties of space.
definitions.example: Figuring out the area of a circle is geometry.

definitions.definition: The physics
